title: The Sherpa Request That Became Hillary's First School at Khumjung
dek: In 1960 Edmund Hillary asked what he could do for the Sherpa people; the answer was a school, and it opened at Khumjung in 1961.

story.event: Building a school at Khumjung after Sherpas asked for one
story.summary: During his 1960-61 expedition to the Everest region, Edmund Hillary asked a Sherpa friend what he could do for the Sherpa people and was asked for a school in Khumjung; the village elders also made a school a condition of lending him the monastery's 'yeti scalp'. Funded from Chicago sponsors for no more than $20,000 by Hillary's estimate, the aluminium school opened in 1961 with about 40 children and a teacher from Darjeeling. More villages asked for schools, and the Himalayan Trust, registered in 1963, went on to build 27.
paragraphs: In 1960 Edmund Hillary was back in the Everest region with a scientific and mountaineering expedition, one that also went looking for evidence of the yeti. Seven years had passed since he and Tenzing Norgay reached the summit. Over his climbing years, he later said, he had grown close to the Sherpa people, and it was obvious to him that they lacked things he took for granted, such as schooling for their children and medical care.

During that visit he asked a Sherpa friend what he could do for the Sherpa people. The Himalayan Trust in Nepal records the answer: "Burra Sahib, our children have eyes but they are blind and cannot see." They wanted a school in Khumjung. Accounts of who spoke differ. Ang Tshering Sherpa, later president of the Nepal Mountaineering Association, has said it was his father, Konchok Chumbi; other tellings name Hillary's sirdar, Urkien, or a boy carrying a petition with sixty children's names. The village elders also made a school one of their conditions for lending Hillary the Khumjung monastery's 'yeti scalp', which turned out to be a fake.

Hillary said yes. "I decided that instead of just thinking about it, why not give them a hand?" he told an interviewer years later. He raised the money in Chicago, from Field Enterprises and from Sears, Roebuck, and reckoned the whole project cost no more than $20,000. The school, a small aluminium building, opened at Khumjung in 1961. He hired a Sherpa teacher from Darjeeling, and by his count it began with 40 children from the village.

Other villages asked next. Schools at Thame and Pangboche were built in 1963, when Khumjung had nearly 70 pupils, and by the Trust's own account Hillary registered the Himalayan Trust in New Zealand that year to handle the growing requests. It went on to build 27 schools, two hospitals and dozens of clinics. Among Khumjung's early pupils were Pertemba Sherpa, who in 1975 climbed Everest by its south-west face, and Ang Rita Sherpa, from its first graduating class, who came to run the Trust in Kathmandu.

quote.text: Such a lamp is our self. So long as it hoards its possessions it keeps itself dark, its conduct contradicts its true purpose. When it finds illumination it forgets itself in a moment, holds the light high, and serves it with everything it has
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Tagore's lamp finds its meaning only when it spends its oil on light. Hillary had a famous name and sponsors who would listen to him; Khumjung's school is what happened when he let the Sherpas tell him where to spend them.

reflection: Hillary did not decide what the Sherpas needed. He asked, and the answer came from people who knew exactly what they wanted for their children. His part was to say yes, find the money and get a building to Khumjung. Within two years, other villages were asking for the same thing.

Tagore's lamp stays dark while it hoards. Whatever you have gathered, whether skill, standing or a name people trust, it may be most useful when someone else tells you where it should shine. Asking them is the simple part, and also the part most often skipped.
invitation: Ask one person you work with or care for a plain question today: if I could do one thing to make your week easier, what would it be? Then listen without suggesting an answer.

cross_checks.claim: Sherpas asked Hillary for a school in Khumjung during his 1960-61 visit
A school was a condition of the Khumjung elders lending the 'yeti scalp', which proved a fake
Schools at Thame and Pangboche followed in 1963
The Himalayan Trust went on to build 27 schools and two hospitals

research_notes: Who asked for the school: Hillary's book Schoolhouse in the Clouds (as cited by Wikipedia) names Sirdar Urkien, asked at a high camp; Ang Tshering Sherpa (UIAA tribute, 2008) says it was his father, Konchok Chumbi; the Himalayan Trust Nepal speaks only of a Sherpa friend, and a Mountain Guides page raising funds with the American Himalayan Foundation of an elderly Sherpa friend; the NZ Herald describes a 15-year-old boy with a petition of 60 names; the Christian Science Monitor and Wikipedia describe the elders' condition attached to the yeti scalp. The story gives the request and lays out the differing accounts rather than choosing one. The quoted reply ('our children have eyes but they are blind and cannot see') is worded thus by the Himalayan Trust Nepal; Ang Tshering's version reads 'can not see' and adds 'We want you to open their eyes by building a school'. First intake: Hillary said 40 children; a search snippet gave 50 but no loaded source supports it, so 40 is used and attributed. Building: Norbu Tenzing describes two aluminium huts, a Mountain Guides page a three-room school, Wikipedia prefabricated aluminium sections flown to Mingbo; the story says only 'a small aluminium building'. Opening month: Wikipedia says mid-June 1961; the story gives the year. Himalayan Trust founding: the Himalayan Trust Nepal says it was registered in New Zealand in 1963, the BBC obituary says 1964, the NZ Herald says it was set up after the first school; the story gives the Trust's own 1963 with attribution. School totals: 27 (Himalayan Trust Nepal, NZ Herald), 26 (Wikipedia), nearly 30 (BBC); the Trust now supports more than 60 schools it did not all build. The CSM opinion piece wrongly calls the 1960 trip Hillary's first return since 1953; that detail is not used. Field Enterprises is named by Hillary as a 1961 funder and by the Himalayan Journal as the 1963 sponsor. Tagore's passage is about the self that finds meaning in giving; it is applied by analogy.
